summary: Presents an abstract protocol framework for securely moving credentials, such as private keys, between devices and credential servers. It responds to requirements listed in RFC 3157, driven by growing numbers and types of Internet devices. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you use several devices, you want your key to follow you safely. This is the outline for a safe locker service that hands it out.

questions: how do roaming users get their private keys
subtitle: A framework for letting roaming users fetch their private keys and certificates from a credential server securely.

tldr.problem: Users want the same private keys and certificates on several devices, including constrained wireless ones that lack import and export tools, without exposing those credentials.
tldr.mechanism: A client and a credential server mutually authenticate, derive a session key, then use three abstract operations, GET, PUT and DELETE, on credentials that are already encrypted as opaque secured credentials.
tldr.outcome: It is an abstract, Informational framework that guides the design of one or more SACRED protocols. It does not define concrete messages.

today: RFC 3760 is an Informational framework from April 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an abstract outline rather than a complete protocol.

sections.title: Credential Mobility
sections.content:
Digital credentials, such as private keys and their certificates, support protocols like S/MIME, IPSec and TLS. Users often want the same credentials on different devices. Desktop tools for import and export exist but are impractical, and on wireless and other constrained devices the tools simply do not exist.

This document proposes a general framework, meeting the requirements of RFC 3157, to guide the development of one or more Securely Available Credentials (SACRED) protocols. It covers client/server exchange; the RFC mentions peer-to-peer exchange as a second architecture but does not describe it.
sections.eli5: Your key is like a house key you want a copy of in every bag. This describes a safe place to keep it so you can collect it wherever you are.

sections.title: Parties, Credentials and Passwords
sections.content:
Three parties take part: the Client, the Credential Server and one or more Credential Stores. Three protocols link them. Protocol 1 (client to server) is the only one this framework describes. Protocols 2 and 3 cover storage access, for example LDAP, and are out of scope.

Credentials may be key pairs, symmetric keys, X.509 and attribute certificates, or application data. They MUST NOT be sent in the clear, so the protocol treats a secured credential as an opaque, privacy and integrity protected object, for example in PKCS#12 or PKCS#15 format. During transfer it gets a second outer encryption layer from a session key, like an encrypted tunnel.

The RFC separates an account password, used to authenticate to the server and negotiate a session key, from a credential password, used to derive a passkey that protects the stored credential. A user may need to remember more than one password.
sections.eli5: Your key goes into a locked box first. For the trip to you, the box is put inside a second locked box that only you and the locker service can open.

sections.title: The GET, PUT and DELETE Operations
sections.content:
A session runs: connect, mutual authentication with key negotiation (using a strong password protocol or equivalent), one or more client requests, server responses, close, then disconnect. Each request must complete before the next. The server SHOULD be willing to serve at least one upload or download after authentication.

Requests use three values: SC-x (the secured credential with a format identifier), Name-x (a user-friendly name, which MUST be unique within an account) and ID-x (a version indicator that SHOULD contain the server's last-modified time). A PUT stores or replaces a credential and returns a new credential-ID. A GET with a credential-ID returns data only if the stored ID does not match, and a GET with no name returns all credentials for the account. A DELETE removes a named credential, optionally only if the ID matches. Uploading a NULL credential is equivalent to removing one.
sections.eli5: You can put a box in the locker, take one out, or throw one away. The version tag stops you from replacing or throwing away the wrong version by accident.

sections.title: Authentication, Formats and Transports
sections.content:
Each SACRED authentication method SHOULD make the server authenticate the client, the client authenticate the server, negotiate a strong session key, and protect the credential exchange with it. The RFC names strong password protocols (such as those in RFC 2945) and TLS, either server-only (sTLS) or with client authentication (cTLS). It warns that TLS server authentication carries risks such as a dishonest certificate authority or faulty certificate chain processing, and that simply layering independently designed security protocols can create a complex protocol open to combined attacks.

A single mandatory-to-implement credential format is needed for portability. The RFC mentions PKCS#12 and PKCS#15 as available. Candidate transports, all built on TCP, are raw TCP, BEEP (RFC 3080) and HTTP (RFC 2616).
sections.eli5: Both sides must prove who they are. You need to know it is the real locker service, and the service needs to know it is really you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Communications need confidentiality (resistant to dictionary attack), integrity (so an update cannot be turned into a deletion or old credentials replayed) and entity authentication. There are no non-repudiation requirements on the protocol itself.

For systems, users should choose passwords with reasonable entropy and clients should avoid echoing them. With TLS, the client interface should let users check the server's X.509 certificate details, and a client SHOULD only be configured with SACRED trust anchors; re-using trust anchors from other applications such as browsers is NOT RECOMMENDED. Servers should salt and super-encrypt verifiers and credentials, resist replay at login, and control or monitor online login attempts. Locking an account after failures can itself enable denial of service, so servers should also watch for abnormal request volumes.
sections.eli5: Pick a hard-to-guess password, check you are talking to the real service, and the service should lock out someone who keeps guessing.

messages.label: mutual authentication
messages.note: Both sides authenticate and negotiate a session key.
